passages.title: The Compass Inside the Bird
passages.text:
Each autumn, hundreds of millions of songbirds leave the forests of northern Europe and Asia and fly south, many of them at night, many of them alone, and most of them making the journey for the first time. A young garden warbler that has never left its birthplace will nevertheless set off in roughly the correct direction, cross a continent and arrive in a wintering area it has never seen. For more than seventy years biologists have been trying to explain how such a bird knows where to go.

The first serious clue emerged in the 1950s, when German researchers placed European robins in circular cages during the migratory season. Even with no view of the sky, the caged birds fluttered persistently towards one side of the cage, and the side they chose corresponded to the direction they would have taken in the wild. When the researchers surrounded the cages with coils that altered the local magnetic field, the birds shifted their preferred direction accordingly. Something in the robin was responding to magnetism.

Later experiments revealed that the avian compass does not work like the compass in a hiker's pocket. A hiker's needle distinguishes north from south by the polarity of the field. A robin, by contrast, appears to read the angle at which the field lines meet the surface of the earth: the lines are steeply inclined near the poles and almost horizontal at the equator. Because the bird detects inclination rather than polarity, it does not sense north and south so much as "poleward" and "equatorward". Reversing the polarity of an artificial field leaves the bird's choice unchanged, whereas tilting the field confuses it completely.

Two candidate mechanisms are now discussed. The first involves a light-sensitive protein called cryptochrome, found in the retina. In this model, blue light striking cryptochrome creates a pair of molecules whose behaviour is subtly influenced by the surrounding magnetic field, so that the bird may effectively see the field as a pattern of shading superimposed on its visual world. The model predicts that the compass should fail in total darkness or under red light alone, and in laboratory tests birds do indeed lose their orientation under those conditions. The second mechanism involves crystals of magnetite, an iron-rich mineral, in tissue of the upper beak, linked to the brain by the trigeminal nerve. Birds whose trigeminal nerve has been temporarily blocked still orient correctly, but they lose the ability to judge magnetic intensity, which suggests that the beak supplies a kind of map rather than a compass.

The magnetic sense, however, is only one instrument in a well-equipped cockpit. Young birds also learn the rotation of the night sky, fixing on the point around which the stars appear to turn, and many species calibrate their various cues against the pattern of polarised light visible at sunset. Experienced adults add a memorised map of coastlines, rivers and, in some cases, odours. The systems overlap and correct one another, which is why removing any single cue rarely stops a bird from migrating.

That redundancy is reassuring, but it is not unlimited. Weak radio-frequency noise of the kind generated by urban electrical equipment has been shown to disrupt the cryptochrome compass in test conditions, and artificial light draws nocturnal migrants off course towards cities. Researchers therefore argue that the electromagnetic and luminous environment of the modern landscape deserves as much conservation attention as its forests and wetlands.

passages.title: The Clock and the Ordering of the Day
passages.text:
Before the fourteenth century, an hour was not a fixed quantity. Following a convention inherited from antiquity, most of Europe divided daylight into twelve parts and darkness into twelve more. Because the amount of daylight changes with the seasons, a summer hour in northern Europe could last well over seventy minutes while a winter hour shrank to little more than forty. These so-called temporal hours suited a society whose work was governed by the sun, and the instruments used to track them, chiefly sundials and water clocks, were adequate for the purpose. Water clocks, however, were awkward: they had to be refilled, they ran differently as the pressure of the water fell, and in the northern winter they froze.

The decisive change was mechanical. Somewhere in western Europe in the last decades of the thirteenth century, an unknown craftsman devised the escapement, a device that releases the energy of a falling weight in small, regular instalments rather than all at once. The earliest form, the verge and foliot, was crude and lost perhaps a quarter of an hour a day, but it had an advantage no water clock could match: it ran at the same rate in January and July, at midnight and at noon. A machine that measured equal intervals made temporal hours impractical, and within a few generations the equal hour had become the standard unit of European time.

The demand for such a machine came first from religious houses. Monastic life was organised around a sequence of daily services, and a community had to be woken and assembled at fixed points during the night. Mechanical alarms that tripped a bell were installed to rouse the sacrist, who then rang the great bell for everyone else. Significantly, the first clocks were valued less for showing the time than for striking it; many early examples had no dial at all.

Towns quickly saw the point. From the 1330s onwards, Italian and then northern cities competed to install public striking clocks in their towers, and a civic clock became a statement of prosperity as much as a public utility. The consequences reached furthest in the cloth towns of Flanders and northern France, where bells began to mark the beginning and end of the working day and the pauses within it. Wages could now be tied to measured time rather than to output alone, and disputes between weavers and their employers increasingly turned on the honesty of the bell. Time had become a commodity that could be sold, wasted or stolen.

Precision improved slowly, then suddenly. For three centuries the mechanism changed little. Then, in 1656, the Dutch mathematician Christiaan Huygens applied the pendulum to clockwork, and the daily error of a good clock fell from minutes to seconds. Only at that point did a minute hand become worth fitting; the second hand followed. Domestic clocks spread through prosperous households in the eighteenth century, and portable watches, at first jewellery for the wealthy, became genuinely accurate instruments as railways created a commercial demand for coordinated schedules.

Historians disagree about how far the clock caused the habits of industrial society and how far it merely served them. What is not disputed is that a technology invented to summon monks to prayer ended by supplying the framework within which factories, timetables and, eventually, the working lives of most of humanity were organised.

passages.title: Bringing the Bogs Back
passages.text:
Peatlands are among the least admired and most valuable landscapes on earth. They occupy roughly three per cent of the planet's land surface, a strip of ground smaller than the area of farmland in a single large country, yet the carbon locked in them is commonly estimated to be about twice that held in all the world's forests. They achieve this not by growing quickly but by decaying slowly.

The mechanism is waterlogging. In a healthy bog the water table sits within a few centimetres of the surface all year round, so that the dead remains of mosses and sedges are submerged almost as soon as they form. Under water there is very little oxygen, and without oxygen the bacteria and fungi that normally break down plant material work at a fraction of their usual speed. The dominant plant of northern bogs, sphagnum moss, actively assists the process: it acidifies the water around it and holds many times its own weight in moisture, creating conditions in which almost nothing rots. Peat therefore accumulates, typically at about a millimetre a year. A bog three metres deep may represent three thousand years of patient, waterlogged accounting.

Drainage reverses that accounting with remarkable speed. Across Europe and South-East Asia, peatlands have been ditched to create pasture, cropland and plantations, and cut for fuel and horticultural compost. Once air reaches the peat, decomposition resumes, and carbon that took millennia to accumulate returns to the atmosphere in decades. Drained and degraded peat is estimated to release around one twentieth of all greenhouse gases produced by human activity, an extraordinary contribution from such a small fraction of the land surface. Dry peat also burns: peat fires can smoulder underground for months, spreading beneath firebreaks and reigniting after rain.

Restoration begins with the simplest of remedies, which is to block the ditches. Dams of peat, plastic piling or timber are installed along drainage channels so that water is retained rather than shed, and the target is to raise the water table to within about ten centimetres of the surface. On sloping ground the work is laborious, requiring hundreds of small dams rather than a few large ones. Bare peat surfaces are then stabilised, often by spreading cut heather or straw and reintroducing sphagnum. Grazing pressure is usually reduced, and self-seeded trees, which pump water out of the ground through their leaves, may be removed.

The results are not immediate and not entirely comfortable. A rewetted bog releases methane, a gas with a far stronger warming effect than carbon dioxide over a twenty-year period, and for the first years after restoration the climate balance sheet can look worse rather than better. Over the longer term, however, the halt in carbon dioxide loss outweighs the methane, and modelling generally shows a net benefit within a few decades. Other gains arrive sooner. Rewetted catchments release water more slowly during storms, reducing downstream flooding, and the water leaving them carries less dissolved carbon, which lowers the cost of treating drinking supplies.

Perhaps the most promising development is the attempt to keep peatlands wet while still farming them, an approach known as paludiculture. Reed, sedge and cattail can be harvested for insulation board, packaging and fuel; sphagnum itself can be cultivated as a peat-free growing medium for the horticultural trade. If such crops can be made profitable, restoration need not depend on subsidy alone. Meanwhile satellites now measure the millimetre-scale rise and fall of bog surfaces as they swell with water and subside in drought, giving managers an early indication of whether a restored site is truly recovering.

passages.title: The Economics of Attention
passages.text:
In 1971 the economist and cognitive scientist Herbert Simon offered an observation that has aged unusually well. A wealth of information, he wrote, creates a poverty of something else, because information consumes the attention of its recipients. Where information is scarce, the valuable thing is information; where information is abundant, the valuable thing is the human capacity to attend to it. Half a century later, an entire industry is organised around that insight.

The business model is straightforward. Most large online platforms are free to use and earn their revenue by selling advertising, so their income rises with the amount of time and engagement they can capture. Engagement is measured through proxies: clicks, shares, comments, dwell time, the proportion of a video watched before the viewer leaves. Recommendation systems are then trained to predict which item, from a catalogue of millions, will maximise those measures for a particular user. The technique is unglamorous statistics rather than mind control. Early systems relied on collaborative filtering, which recommends to one user what similar users have chosen, while modern versions combine hundreds of signals in models that are retrained continuously.

Critics argue that optimising for engagement has predictable side effects. Material that provokes strong emotion, particularly outrage, tends to travel further than material that is merely accurate, so a system that rewards attention may systematically favour the sensational. A related concern is the filter bubble: if a system shows people only what they already agree with, public debate fragments into isolated communities that share no common set of facts. The argument is intuitive, and it has shaped a decade of public discussion.

The evidence, though, is more complicated than the rhetoric. Several large studies have found that the news diets of ordinary users are more varied than the bubble metaphor suggests, partly because most people consume relatively little political content and partly because social feeds expose them to material shared by acquaintances with different views. Some researchers conclude that self-selection matters more than algorithmic curation: people choose their sources, and the algorithm mostly reflects those choices back to them. Others reply that averages conceal the small minority of heavy users among whom effects are strongest, and that experiments lasting a few weeks cannot capture changes that unfold over years. The honest summary is that the direction of the effect is contested and its size is probably smaller than commonly assumed, though not zero.

Meanwhile the design remedies have multiplied. Some platforms now offer chronological rather than ranked feeds, publish dashboards showing time spent, or introduce small points of friction, such as prompting a user to open an article before sharing it. Evaluations of such measures are mixed: friction reliably reduces sharing, but reduced sharing is not the same as better-informed readers. Regulators in several jurisdictions have taken a different route, requiring platforms above a certain size to disclose how their ranking systems work and to grant vetted researchers access to data, on the reasonable principle that a phenomenon cannot be governed until it can be measured.

There is also a quieter, individual response. Sustained attention appears to be, in part, a trainable capacity, and habits such as reading long texts without interruption, keeping devices out of the room while working and batching messages into fixed periods are widely recommended by psychologists. None of this is a substitute for institutional reform. But it is a reminder that attention is not only a commodity that others buy and sell; it is also the medium in which a person's own thinking is done.

passages.title: The Street at Eye Level
passages.text:
Ask an architect what makes a street worth walking along and the answer is likely to involve proportion, materials or skyline. Ask the people actually walking, and the reply, according to fifty years of observational research, is decided much lower down: in the narrow band of building frontage between the pavement and the first floor. Above that band, this tradition argues, the pedestrian barely looks.

The claim rests on counting. Observers position themselves on a corner with a hand counter and record how many people pass, how quickly they move, how often they stop and what they do when they stop. Surveys carried out in Copenhagen, Melbourne and New York have produced a consistent pattern. Walkers slow down and linger in front of active frontage, such as shopfronts, cafes, workshops and residential entrances, and they accelerate along blank walls, service bays and long unbroken facades. In one comparison, average walking speed beside a blank wall was about a third higher than beside an equivalent run of small shops, while the number of people who paused fell almost tenfold. The density of doorways, rather than the density of housing, proved to be the single strongest predictor of street life.

Why the effect should be so strong is a question of attention rather than architecture. A person walking at a comfortable pace covers a hundred metres in a little over a minute. If that hundred metres contains one entrance and a single sheet of tinted glass, the walk supplies one event; if it contains fifteen small units, something new appears every few seconds. Psychologists studying environmental preference report that people rate finely grained facades as more interesting and less tiring, and that the same route feels shorter when it is visually eventful. Blankness, in other words, is not neutral. It lengthens the perceived distance and encourages people to leave.

Several cities have translated the finding into regulation. Rather than prescribing a style, the newer codes prescribe performance at ground level: a maximum width for individual ground-floor units, a minimum number of entrances per hundred metres of frontage, a required proportion of transparent glazing rather than mirrored or shuttered panels, and limits on the length of any single blank surface. Melbourne and Amsterdam both operate scoring systems in which every block of frontage is graded from active to hostile, and planning consent for large developments is tied to the score achieved.

The approach has its critics. The most serious objection is that the relationship may run backwards: shops open where people already are, so the correlation between lively frontage and lively streets may record the cause rather than the effect. A second objection is commercial. As retail moves online, requiring every ground floor to be a shop risks producing rows of empty units that are deader than the blank wall they replaced, and some planners now argue for frontage that can be occupied by workshops, clinics, nurseries or housing with a genuine front door. There is also the danger of what one critic calls facade theatre, in which the required glazing is duly installed and then papered over from the inside.

Frontage, in any case, is only part of the picture. The same observational tradition measures where people sit, and finds that the quantity and placement of seating governs how long anyone stays. People occupy the edges of a square before its centre, preferring a back that is protected and a view that is open, and they choose shade in hot climates and sun in cool ones. The most telling statistic for a public space, on this view, is not how many people cross it, but how many choose to remain.

passages.title: Concrete That Repairs Itself
passages.text:
Concrete is the most widely used manufactured material on earth, and it cracks. Some cracking is unavoidable: the material shrinks as it cures, expands and contracts with temperature, and carries loads that put its weakest side in tension. Hairline cracks a fraction of a millimetre wide do little harm in themselves, but they open a path for water and, near roads or coasts, for chlorides. Once these reach the steel reinforcement inside, the steel corrodes, and because rust occupies more volume than the metal it replaces, it forces the surrounding concrete apart. Much of the money spent on bridges and tunnels goes not on building them but on finding and sealing such cracks before that sequence begins.

Concrete has always had a modest capacity to repair itself. A typical mix contains more cement than the available water can hydrate, so unreacted grains remain scattered through the hardened material for years. When a crack lets in moisture, those grains hydrate and swell, and dissolved calcium reacts with carbon dioxide to deposit a thin crust. This autogenous healing is real but limited: it closes cracks up to roughly 0.2 millimetres and stops there.

The engineering ambition is to extend the effect deliberately. The best known approach is biological. Spores of alkali-tolerant bacteria, together with a calcium-based nutrient, are packed into porous clay pellets and mixed into the wet concrete, where they survive the high alkalinity of the material and remain dormant, in principle for decades. A crack admits water and oxygen; the spores then germinate, consume the nutrient and precipitate calcium carbonate, in effect growing limestone across the gap. Laboratory specimens have sealed cracks close to a millimetre wide, and the sealed material recovers much of its resistance to water, though not all of its original strength.

Two mechanical strategies compete with the biological one. In vascular systems, hollow tubes or channels filled with an adhesive are cast into the structure; a crack ruptures them, the liquid bleeds into the void and hardens, and the network can in principle be refilled from outside. Microcapsule systems disperse the same idea as millions of tiny shells, which release their contents once and cannot be replenished. A simpler option uses superabsorbent polymer grains, which swell on contact with water and physically plug the crack while the slower chemistry of the concrete works behind them.

None of this is free. Bacterial concrete costs substantially more than a conventional mix, and the pellets that carry the spores are weaker than the aggregate they displace, so the concrete is measurably less strong when new. Vascular networks complicate casting and are difficult to arrange inside a heavily reinforced beam. Testing is a further obstacle, because standards were written for materials whose properties are fixed at twenty-eight days, and a specification cannot easily reward a benefit that first appears in year fifteen. Field trials remain small: an irrigation channel and a lock wall in the Netherlands, sections of tunnel lining, a handful of retaining walls.

The case for persevering is arithmetic. Cement production accounts for something in the region of seven per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and the cheapest way to cut that figure is to build less, which in practice means making structures last longer. A material that doubles the service life of a bridge deck is worth a considerable premium, even if it never seals a single crack that a skilled inspector could not have found.

passages.title: Part 1: Hiring a room at a community centre
passages.script:
MAN: Good morning, Riverside Community Centre, Tom speaking.
WOMAN: Oh, hello. I'm hoping to hire a room for a family party, and I wondered whether you had anything free in September.
MAN: I'm sure we can help. Can I take a few details first? What name is it?
WOMAN: It's Helen Braithwaite.
MAN: Could you spell the surname for me?
WOMAN: Yes, it's B-R-A-I-T-H-W-A-I-T-E. Braithwaite.
MAN: Thank you. And the best number to reach you on?
WOMAN: My mobile, 07811 493 625.
MAN: 07811 493 625. And what sort of event is it?
WOMAN: It's my parents' wedding anniversary, so we're expecting a lot of older guests.
MAN: Noted. And which date were you thinking of?
WOMAN: We'd like Saturday the 14th of September, if that's possible. The following Saturday would be too late for us.
MAN: Let me look. Yes, the 14th is still free in two of our rooms. There's the Oak Room, which seats 40 people, and the Willow Room, which seats 85.
WOMAN: We've invited about 60, so it will have to be the Willow Room.
MAN: Right, the Willow Room. That's 90 pounds for an evening booking, and an evening booking runs from 6 until 11.
WOMAN: Does that include time to clear up afterwards?
MAN: Everything has to be out of the building by half past eleven, and we don't charge for that extra half hour. We do ask for a deposit of 25 pounds when you book, and you get that back afterwards if there's no damage.
WOMAN: That sounds fair. Is there a kitchen we can use?
MAN: There is, but I should warn you that it's a serving kitchen. You can't actually cook in it. There's a large fridge, a dishwasher and an oven for reheating food, and that's all anybody uses it for.
WOMAN: We're having the food delivered anyway, so that's not a problem. What about parking?
MAN: We have 22 spaces in our own car park, and after 6 in the evening you can park free on Mill Lane itself.
WOMAN: Sorry, could you give me the full address? I need it for the invitations.
MAN: Of course. We're at 12 Mill Lane, and the postcode is B S 4, 2 J P.
WOMAN: Thank you. So what happens next?
MAN: I'll email you a booking form this afternoon. Fill it in, send it back with the deposit within 7 days, and the room is yours. Oh, and one thing people always forget: the music has to stop at 10.45, because of the neighbours. Guests can stay until 11, but the sound system goes off at quarter to.
WOMAN: That's fine. Most of them will be leaving before that anyway. I'll watch out for your email.
MAN: You're welcome. Goodbye.

passages.title: Part 2: Welcome talk at the Old Granary Arts Centre
passages.script:
WOMAN: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Old Granary Arts Centre. My name is Priya and I look after visitor services, so I'll take five minutes to explain how the building works before you go off and explore it for yourselves.

The Granary was built in 1878 to store grain that came up the canal from the docks. It stood empty for almost forty years, and the conversion took 3 years. We opened to the public last spring. Almost everything you can see is original: the brickwork, the iron columns and the timber floors.

There are four floors, and the easiest way to see them is to take the lift to the top and then walk down. The top floor is our cafe, which is called the Loft. It serves hot lunches until half past two and closes at 4 o'clock. It is also the only place in the building where you may eat or drink, so please don't carry cups of coffee into the galleries with you.

The third floor is the main exhibition space. At the moment it is showing photographs of the canal taken between 1930 and 1975, and that exhibition runs until the 30th of November. Entry to the third floor costs 6 pounds, or 4 pounds for students and for anyone over sixty. The ground floor gallery, by contrast, is completely free, and that is where we show work by local artists.

The second floor is our teaching space. We run courses in printmaking, ceramics and photography up there, and materials are included in the course fee. The most popular session by far is the life drawing class on Thursday evenings, which begins at 7. That one doesn't need to be booked. You simply turn up with a pencil.

A few practical points. There are lockers by the main entrance and they take a 1 pound coin, which you get back when you collect your things. You are very welcome to take photographs anywhere in the building, but please switch the flash off, because some of the older prints are extremely fragile. Guided tours leave the reception desk at 11 and again at 2, and they last about forty-five minutes.

Finally, if you think you are likely to come back, membership is worth considering. It costs 45 pounds a year and it gives you free entry to every paid exhibition, ten per cent off everything in the shop, and an invitation to our opening evenings. You can join at the desk on your way out, or on our website.

Right. The lift is behind you on the left, and I shall be in the foyer until five if anybody has questions.

passages.title: Part 3: Tutorial on a food waste project
passages.script:
TUTOR: Come in, Daniel. Sit down. So, how is the food waste project coming along?
DANIEL: Better than it was last month, I think. I've narrowed it down to halls of residence rather than the whole city, which makes it much more manageable.
TUTOR: That's a sensible decision. Remind me what your central question is.
DANIEL: Whether students in catered halls throw away more food than students who cook for themselves. My expectation is that the self-catered students waste more, because they buy in quantities that are too big for one person.
TUTOR: That's a reasonable hypothesis, but be prepared to find the opposite. How are you collecting the data?
DANIEL: Originally I was going to weigh the bins in every shared kitchen, but the cleaning contractor wouldn't agree to it. So I've moved to food diaries instead. 50 students keep a diary for one week and write down everything they throw away.
TUTOR: Diaries can work well, but you know their weakness.
DANIEL: People forget to fill them in?
TUTOR: People forget, and, rather more seriously, people change their behaviour because they know they are being observed. Your figures will almost certainly be too low. I'd rather you said so plainly in your limitations section than hoped nobody would notice.
DANIEL: I'll write that in. I'm also running a short questionnaire with a much larger group, 120 students, about their shopping habits, so I'll have something to set the diaries against.
TUTOR: Good. Have you piloted the questionnaire?
DANIEL: Not yet. I was planning to send it out next week.
TUTOR: Don't. Test it on 10 people first, this week if you possibly can. Every year somebody discovers a badly worded question after two hundred people have already answered it. And have you submitted the ethics form?
DANIEL: I sent it off on Monday. The department office said it usually takes 2 weeks.
TUTOR: Then you cannot collect a single piece of data until it comes back, so plan around that. What about your reading?
DANIEL: I've read the Watson paper you recommended, and one or two things on supermarket packaging.
TUTOR: Watson is the obvious starting point, but remember that her study looks at households with children, so you can't simply transfer her conclusions to students without saying why. Look at the chapter by Okonkwo as well. It's on the reading list and it deals specifically with young adults living alone for the first time.
DANIEL: Okonkwo. I'll find it this week. Can I also ask about the length? Somebody told me it was four thousand words.
TUTOR: It's 5000 words, excluding the appendices and the bibliography, and the deadline is the 6th of March, which is a Friday. There is also a presentation in the last week of term. 10 minutes, plus questions from the group.
DANIEL: Ten minutes on the whole project?
TUTOR: On the method and the findings. Nobody wants to hear the literature review a second time. Send me your draft questionnaire by Friday and I'll look at it over the weekend.
DANIEL: Thank you. That's really helpful.

passages.title: The Box That Shrank the World
passages.text:
A
For most of the industrial age the great bottleneck in world trade was not the ocean but the edge of it. A ship crossing the Atlantic in 1950 could make the passage in ten days and then sit at a wharf for a week or more while gangs of dockers moved its cargo piece by piece. Everything travelled in its own packaging: sacks of coffee, barrels of oil, crates of machinery, bales of cotton, each of a different size and weight, each needing to be lifted, carried, stacked and wedged by hand. Estimates from the period suggest that handling in port could swallow as much as half of the total cost of sending a consignment overseas. Distance, in other words, was cheap. It was arrival that was expensive.

B
The solution, when it came, was not a technological marvel. It was a box. In 1956 an American road haulier called Malcom McLean, who had spent years watching his lorries queue at the docks in New Jersey, loaded fifty-eight metal trailer bodies onto the deck of a converted tanker and sent them to Houston. Nothing about the box itself was ingenious; welded steel and a pair of doors had been available for decades. What was ingenious was the thought behind it, which was that the unit of shipping should no longer be the individual product but a standard container that need not be opened at any point between the factory gate and the customer's warehouse. At a stroke, cargo handling stopped being the movement of goods and became the movement of boxes, a task that machines can do far better than people.

C
The savings were immediate and startling, and yet the idea spread slowly, because a container is worthless on its own. It is only useful as part of a system that includes cranes tall enough to lift it, chassis built to carry it, railway wagons designed to take it and acres of paved ground on which to stack it. Dockers' unions, meanwhile, could see exactly what was coming; waterfront employment in several major ports fell by more than two thirds within twenty years, and long disputes over manning levels and redundancy payments delayed adoption in Britain, Australia and the United States. Shipping lines added a further obstacle by building boxes to their own dimensions, so that a container from one carrier could not be stacked securely on another's vessel.

D
What broke the deadlock was an agreement about details. During the 1960s a series of international committees settled on a small family of standard lengths, of which the twenty-foot and forty-foot units became dominant, together with fixed heights, widths and, most importantly, a fixed pattern of steel corner castings. Into those castings fits a twist-lock, a rotating steel cone that secures a box to a crane, to a lorry chassis or to the box beneath it. It is the least glamorous component in the whole apparatus and arguably the most consequential, because it is what makes the container interchangeable rather than merely large.

E
Military logistics supplied the first great proving ground. Supplying American forces in Vietnam was a formidable problem of distance and volume, and the armed forces contracted for container services on a scale no commercial route could then match. That business had an unintended consequence. Ships returning eastward across the Pacific were empty, and their operators went looking for anything that would fill them. What they found was a Japanese manufacturing sector eager to reach American consumers. The transpacific trade in cameras, televisions and, later, cars grew out of a search for return cargo.

F
The consequences on land were just as far-reaching. Old docks lay in the middle of cities, hemmed in by warehouses and narrow streets, with no room for the storage yards the new system demanded. Traffic therefore migrated to deepwater sites with space to expand and good road links: Felixstowe rather than London, Rotterdam rather than Amsterdam, Newark rather than Manhattan. The map of world shipping was quietly redrawn, and a port's fortunes came to depend less on the hinterland it served than on the depth of its water and the ambition of its planners.

G
Quantifying the effect on trade itself has proved harder. Freight rates fell steeply, but so did tariffs, and air travel, telephones and computers were transforming commerce at the same moment. One econometric study of trade flows between industrial countries concluded that adopting containers had a larger effect on the volume of goods exchanged than the tariff reductions negotiated over the same decades. What is beyond dispute is that cheap, reliable, predictable freight allowed manufacturers to break production into stages and place each stage wherever it was cheapest. Supply chains that assumed goods would arrive on a known day were possible only because the box had made arrival boring.

H
The system has since developed problems of its own. Ships have grown to carry more than twenty thousand containers, forcing ports into ever deeper dredging and leaving terminals overwhelmed when several giants dock at once. Roughly one container movement in five is an empty box being repositioned to where the next load waits. The virtue of the container is that it is indifferent to what it holds; that indifference is also its weakness.

passages.title: What the Sleeping Brain Rehearses
passages.text:
A
Sleep looks like an absence. The eyes close, the muscles relax, awareness of the room disappears, and for most of human history the obvious conclusion was that the brain had shut down for the night. Recording electrodes have made that conclusion untenable. The sleeping brain is not switched off but switched over, running patterns of activity that never occur in waking life and consuming almost as much energy as it does when awake. The question that has occupied researchers for half a century is what all that activity is for, and the most persuasive answer so far concerns memory.

B
A night's sleep is not uniform. Within minutes of falling asleep a person descends into the lighter stages of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep, then into deep slow-wave sleep, in which large, slow electrical waves sweep across the cortex roughly once a second. Riding on those waves are short bursts of faster rhythm known as spindles, each lasting about a second and generated in a structure at the centre of the brain. Later in the night the pattern shifts towards rapid-eye-movement sleep, in which the brain's electrical signature resembles that of waking, the eyes flick beneath the lids, most vivid dreaming occurs and the muscles of the body are temporarily paralysed. A sleeper cycles through this sequence four or five times, with slow-wave sleep dominating the first half of the night and rapid-eye-movement sleep the second.

C
The earliest experimental hint that sleep does something for memory came in the 1920s, when two American psychologists asked volunteers to learn lists of nonsense syllables and tested them after equal intervals of sleep or wakefulness. Those who had slept remembered more. For decades the standard explanation was passive: sleep protects fragile new memories simply by preventing the flood of new experience that would otherwise interfere with them. On that view the sleeping brain deserves no credit at all; it merely stays out of the way. The passive account is elegant, and it is almost certainly incomplete.

D
Evidence for a more active process came from rats. When a rat explores a maze, particular cells in the hippocampus fire as it passes particular locations, producing a recognisable sequence of activity for each route. During subsequent slow-wave sleep the same sequences reappear, in the same order but compressed into a fraction of the original time and repeated many times over. This phenomenon, known as replay, is accompanied by bursts of hippocampal activity that are precisely timed to the slow waves and spindles of the cortex. The favoured interpretation is that the hippocampus, which learns quickly but holds little, is rehearsing the day's episodes to the cortex, which learns slowly but stores for years. Sleep, on this account, is when a temporary record is copied into a permanent one.

E
If replay matters, then influencing it should influence what is remembered. This is the reasoning behind targeted memory reactivation. Volunteers learn the positions of objects on a screen while a particular odour is present, or while each object is paired with a distinctive sound. When the same odour or sound is delivered quietly during slow-wave sleep, memory for the associated items is measurably better the following morning than for items whose cues were not replayed. The effect is modest and it does not work for everything, but it has been reproduced in many laboratories, and it is difficult to explain without granting the sleeping brain an active role. Individual differences point the same way: people whose recordings show more spindles after learning tend to retain more, and a daytime nap of ninety minutes can produce benefits comparable to a night.

F
Rapid-eye-movement sleep appears to do something different. Where slow-wave sleep seems to stabilise memories more or less as they were formed, rapid-eye-movement sleep is associated with recombining them. Volunteers woken from it are better at solving anagrams and at spotting remote connections between words than those woken from other stages, and studies of problem-solving report that a night containing plenty of it increases the chance of noticing a hidden rule in a task learned the day before. There is also evidence that this stage helps drain the emotional charge from unpleasant memories while leaving their content intact, which would explain why distressing events often feel less raw after a few nights and why disturbed sleep is a feature of so many psychiatric conditions.

G
Deprivation experiments approach the question from the other end. A person kept awake for a night before learning encodes new information markedly less well, and imaging shows reduced activity in exactly the hippocampal regions that ordinarily support encoding. The deficit is not simply tiredness, since it persists when volunteers are given stimulants that restore alertness on other tasks.

H
Caution is still warranted. Much of the evidence links laboratory tasks to laboratory sleep, and remembering the position of a picture on a screen is not the same as understanding a chapter of history. Yet the direction of travel is consistent, and it has begun to influence practical decisions: a number of school districts that shifted their start times later have reported improvements in attendance and grades. Whatever else it is for, sleep is not idleness. It is the shift during which the day's raw material is sorted, and some of it is thrown away.

passages.title: The Return of the River Engineer
passages.text:
A
Europe once had beavers in almost every river system that could support them, and then, for several centuries, it had almost none. The animal was hunted for three separate products: a dense waterproof fur, a meat that the medieval church was willing to classify as fish and therefore permit during fasts, and castoreum, a bitter secretion from glands near the tail that apothecaries prescribed for headaches. By 1900 the continental population had fallen to a few hundred individuals surviving in isolated pockets in Norway, France, Germany and Russia. In Britain the species disappeared entirely, probably by the sixteenth century. Protection, restocking and, later, deliberate reintroduction have reversed that decline; there are now well over a million beavers in Europe, and populations are established or expanding in more than twenty countries.

B
What makes the beaver interesting is not that it has come back but what it does when it arrives. A beaver is a modifier of habitat on a scale matched by few animals other than ourselves. It fells trees along the bank, both for food and for building material, and dams small watercourses to create a pond deep enough that the entrance to its lodge stays underwater in winter. Where the ground is flat it digs canals to float timber from further inland. None of this is done for the benefit of other species. It is a side effect of an animal making a stretch of river safe for itself.

C
The hydrological consequences of that side effect are what have attracted the attention of governments. Water that would have run off a hillside in a few hours is instead held back in ponds and saturated soils and released over days. Monitoring at a small experimental catchment in south-west England found that peak flows leaving a fenced beaver enclosure were substantially lower than those entering it, and that the delay between rainfall and peak was longer. In dry periods the same storage works in reverse, keeping water in headwaters that would otherwise stop flowing. Sediment washed off farmland settles in the ponds along with the nutrients bound to it, so that water leaving a beaver-modified reach is often clearer and carries less phosphate than water entering it.

D
Biodiversity gains follow from the same physical changes. Standing water, dead wood and open sunlit gaps in bankside woodland are exactly the conditions that have become scarce in a tidy, drained landscape. Amphibians breed in the shallow margins of beaver ponds in numbers that can be an order of magnitude greater than in adjacent unmodified streams. The effect on fish is more contested. Anglers' organisations have argued that dams obstruct migrating salmon and trout, while ecologists point to studies showing juvenile fish growing faster in the food-rich water of the ponds, and note that beaver dams are leaky, seasonal structures rather than the concrete weirs that genuinely block a river.

E
Where beavers and people share a floodplain, conflict is inevitable. A dam raises the water table upstream, and land that a farmer has drained at considerable expense may become waterlogged. Culverts under roads and railways are, from a beaver's point of view, ideal places to build, and a blocked culvert can flood a carriageway. Orchards and amenity trees are felled overnight. Burrowing into flood embankments weakens them. These are real costs, they fall on individuals rather than on the public that enjoys the benefits, and the case for reintroduction is not helped when its advocates treat them as trivial.

F
A body of practical management has therefore grown up around the animal. Flow devices, which are pipes laid through a dam with their intakes placed where the beaver cannot detect the sound and movement of escaping water, allow a pond to be held at a chosen level rather than removed. Metal grilles keep the animals out of culverts. Wire mesh or a slurry of sand and paint protects valuable individual trees. Riparian buffer strips, left uncultivated along the water's edge, reduce the chance of conflict by giving beavers food and building material without taking anything a farmer values.

G
Reintroduction has also raised awkward questions of law and definition. Is an animal absent for four hundred years native or alien? In Britain the argument was settled administratively, with the species recognised as native and given protected status, but only after a decade in which unlicensed releases created populations that regulators then had to decide whether to remove. Some ecologists regard those releases as vandalism; others point out that they produced the very populations that made the scientific case. Licensing now attempts to steer new releases towards catchments where the hydrological benefit is greatest and the agricultural conflict least.

H
The wider significance of the beaver lies in what it suggests about restoration itself. Conventional river restoration is expensive, engineered and static: a channel is re-meandered, gravels are placed, and the result is fixed at the moment of construction. A beaver produces a system that keeps changing, abandoning ponds that silt up, moving upstream, letting old dams fail. Ecologists call this process-led restoration, the idea being to reinstate the forces that create habitat rather than the habitat itself. It is cheaper, it is more resilient, and it is considerably harder for a public body to plan, because nobody can say in advance exactly what the river will look like in ten years. That uncertainty, rather than any biological difficulty, may be the real obstacle.

passages.title: A History Written in Salt
passages.text:
A
Salt is the most elusive of the ancient commodities. Pottery breaks but survives, metal corrodes but leaves a stain in the soil, grain chars and can be identified two thousand years later from a single burnt seed. Salt does none of these things. It dissolves in the first rain that reaches it, so that the substance itself is essentially never recovered from an ordinary excavation. Everything archaeologists know about the salt trade has therefore been reconstructed from the things that surrounded it: the vessels used to make it, the tools used to cut it, the settlements that grew rich on it and the texts that taxed it. The subject is a standing demonstration that absence of evidence and evidence of absence are different things.

B
The most abundant of those indirect traces is a crude, gritty, low-fired ceramic known as briquetage. Along the coasts of Atlantic Europe, and around inland brine springs from Poland to the English Midlands, excavators encounter mounds of it, sometimes several metres deep, composed of fragments of coarse cylindrical containers, pedestals and bars. The technique they represent was simple. Sea water or spring brine was concentrated, by evaporation in shallow pans or by filtering it through salt-laden sand or ash, and then poured into the containers, which were supported on the pedestals over a fire until the water had gone. What remained was a solid loaf of salt in the shape of its vessel, which was broken to release it. Every kilogram of salt therefore destroyed a pot, which is why the debris is measured in hillsides rather than in sherds.

C
Rock salt allowed an entirely different industry, and the Austrian site of Hallstatt is its classic illustration. Miners there drove galleries into a salt-bearing mountain from the Bronze Age onwards, cutting the mineral with bronze picks and hauling it out in leather rucksacks and wooden troughs. Because salt is a superb preservative and the workings stayed dry, the mine has returned material that survives almost nowhere else from the period: woollen textiles in patterned weaves, fur caps, plaited ropes, wooden staircases, torch fragments. A workplace has been preserved rather than a grave, which is unusual, and it shows an operation organised on an industrial scale, with a division of labour and a community around it.

D
Brine wells produced a third tradition. In Sichuan, drillers sank narrow shafts by repeatedly dropping a weighted iron bit suspended from a bamboo cable, a percussion technique that reached depths of several hundred metres by the eleventh century and more than a kilometre by the nineteenth. Brine was raised in long bamboo tubes and evaporated in iron pans, and natural gas encountered in the same shafts was piped through bamboo to fire them. The engineering was far in advance of anything in contemporary Europe, and nineteenth-century western drillers borrowed from it directly.

E
Why so much effort was invested is a question with more than one answer. A common textbook explanation is dietary: human beings need sodium, and agricultural diets based on grain and vegetables supply less of it than a diet of meat and milk. That is true as far as it goes, but the quantities produced at major sites far exceed what any plausible local population needed to stay healthy, so physiological need cannot be the whole story. The stronger explanation is preservation. Salted fish, salted meat and salt-fermented sauces allowed a summer's catch to be eaten in winter and a coastal surplus to be traded inland, which turns a perishable resource into a storable one and, in effect, into wealth.

F
That transformation had political consequences. Where a commodity is essential, bulky and produced at a small number of identifiable places, it is easy to tax and tempting to monopolise. Salt duties financed states from Han China to Bourbon France, whose notoriously uneven gabelle taxed the same substance at wildly different rates from one province to the next and made smuggling a mass occupation. Control of production sites shaped settlement patterns and roads; several European towns whose names contain a salt element grew up where a route crossed a brine spring.

G
Modern methods have begun to fill some of the gaps. Trace elements and isotopes can sometimes distinguish salt made from sea water from salt made from rock or spring brine, so that a residue inside a storage jar hundreds of kilometres from any coast can occasionally be traced to its source. Experimental archaeology has been just as informative: teams reproducing briquetage in working replicas have found the process ferociously demanding of fuel, requiring several kilograms of wood for every kilogram of salt, which implies managed woodland, seasonal work and a labour force released from other tasks. The picture that emerges is less like a cottage industry and more like a factory that happened to be built of clay and firewood.

H
None of this would be visible if archaeologists had waited for the commodity itself to turn up. The salt trade has had to be inferred, from broken pots, discarded picks, tax registers and the shapes of old roads, and the inference has proved robust enough to support a whole economic history. The most important things in an ancient economy may well be the ones that leave the faintest mark.

passages.title: The Arithmetic of Expertise
passages.text:
A
Few findings in psychology have travelled further from their origins than the claim that ten thousand hours of practice will make anyone an expert. The number came from a study of violin students at a German conservatory, in which the most accomplished group had accumulated roughly that much solitary practice by the age of twenty while less accomplished groups had accumulated less. The original authors made a careful argument about the quality and quantity of training; a popular book a decade later turned it into a slogan, and the slogan turned into a rule. Within a few years the figure was being quoted in management seminars, on sports pitches and in parenting manuals, generally by people who had never read the paper and often in support of claims its authors had explicitly declined to make.

B
It is worth separating the slogan from the science, because the underlying concept is more interesting than the number. Deliberate practice, as the term is used technically, is not the same as experience or even as effort. It refers to activity designed specifically to improve performance, usually by a teacher, undertaken at the limit of what the learner can currently do, accompanied by immediate feedback and repeated with correction. Playing through a favourite piece for an hour is practice; working for an hour on the four bars that fall apart, slowly, with a metronome and a recording device, is deliberate practice. Almost everyone finds the second kind unpleasant, which is one reason why so few people do very much of it.

C
The strong version of the theory holds that differences in accumulated deliberate practice account for most of the differences in performance between individuals in a domain, and that innate talent plays little part. Professor Elena Marchetti, who has defended a version of this position for thirty years, argues that when researchers look closely at prodigies they usually find an unusual training history rather than an unusual brain, and that the belief in talent is socially corrosive because it gives learners permission to stop.

D
The strong claim invited measurement, and measurement has not been kind to it. A meta-analysis assembled by Daniel Okonkwo and colleagues pooled dozens of studies across music, sport, games, education and the professions, and calculated how much of the variation in performance accumulated practice could explain. The answers were consistent and modest: about a quarter in games such as chess, roughly a fifth in music, rather less in sport, and close to nothing in professional occupations such as medicine and law. Practice mattered everywhere and was decisive nowhere.

E
Part of the answer is that the measurements are difficult and the studies are flawed in ways that cut in both directions. Most rely on retrospective diaries, and people are poor at reconstructing how many hours they spent practising a decade ago; those who ended up successful may well remember more. Causation is hard to pin down, since a child who improves quickly is rewarded, encouraged and given better teaching, and therefore practises more, so practice is as much a consequence of early progress as a cause of later attainment. Critics of the strong claim have sometimes ignored these problems when they favour their own case.

F
A second part of the answer concerns the character of the domain. Sofia Grunberg has argued that skill develops reliably through repetition only in what she calls regular environments, where the rules are stable, the same situation recurs and feedback arrives quickly and unambiguously. Chess, classical music and surgery are largely of this kind. Stock picking, long-range political forecasting and clinical psychiatry are not; the environment shifts, feedback is delayed and noisy, and experience may deliver confidence without accuracy. On this account the argument about practice is partly an argument about which domains people happen to study, and generalisations from chess to the rest of human achievement should be treated with suspicion.

G
Then there are the individual differences that practice does not eliminate. Working memory capacity predicts early progress in several complex skills, and although its advantage narrows with training it does not always disappear. Age of starting matters in domains involving perceptual timing. Motivation, temperament and tolerance of tedium determine who is willing to do the unpleasant kind of practice at all, and these are themselves partly heritable, which produces the awkward conclusion that the capacity to practise may be one of the things people are unequally endowed with. Access matters too, and here the research has been strangely quiet: a young musician's hours depend on an instrument, a teacher and a household able to pay for both.

H
My own view is that the public debate has been trapped in a false choice. The interesting question was never whether talent or practice matters more, since neither operates without the other, but how they interact: which kinds of training suit which learners, at which stage, and what a teacher should do when a pupil stops improving. The slogan, meanwhile, has done both harm and good. It has fostered unrealistic promises and a certain cruelty towards those who work hard and remain ordinary. It has also persuaded a great many people that improvement is possible and that method matters more than the accident of a first attempt, which is, on balance, a belief worth having.

passages.title: The Unfinished Physics of Glass
passages.text:
A
Glass is the most familiar material that nobody fully understands. It fills our windows, carries the world's data as optical fibre, holds our drinks and covers the screen in almost every pocket, and yet the question of what it actually is remains genuinely open. A persistent piece of folklore holds that glass is a liquid that flows imperceptibly, and that the thicker bases of medieval cathedral windows are the proof. The folklore is wrong. Those panes are uneven because of how they were made, and glaziers generally set the heavier edge at the bottom; a calculation of the flow expected at room temperature gives a displacement too small to measure over the lifetime of the universe.

B
Consider what happens when a liquid is cooled. Normally, at a particular temperature, its molecules arrange themselves into the repeating lattice of a crystal, and the transition is sharp: heat is released, volume jumps, and the material is unmistakably a solid. But if certain liquids are cooled quickly enough, the molecules cannot organise themselves in time. They keep the disordered arrangement of a liquid while their movement becomes ever more sluggish. Over a modest range of temperature the viscosity climbs by something like fourteen orders of magnitude, until the material flows so slowly that on any human timescale it is a solid. The temperature at which this happens is called the glass transition, and it is not a true transition in the usual sense at all, since where it falls depends on how fast the sample was cooled.

C
This is the heart of the difficulty. When water freezes, the change in behaviour is accompanied by an obvious change in structure. When a glass forms, the structure barely changes: X-ray and neutron measurements of a glass and of the liquid it came from look almost identical, and no growing region of order can be seen. Something has clearly happened, because the material has stopped flowing, but nothing appears to have happened to the arrangement of its atoms. A related puzzle arises from measurements of entropy, the quantity that expresses disorder. As a supercooled liquid is cooled, its entropy falls faster than that of the corresponding crystal, and simple extrapolation suggests that at some finite temperature it would fall below the crystal's, which is very hard to make sense of.

D
Two broad families of explanation compete. Thermodynamic theories propose that the observed transition is the blurred shadow of a genuine one hidden below it, at which the material would settle into an ideal glass, a unique disordered state of minimum entropy that can never quite be reached because reaching it would take infinite time. Kinetic theories deny that any hidden transition exists and treat glassiness as a purely dynamic phenomenon, in which each molecule becomes caged by its neighbours and rearrangement requires ever larger groups to move together. On this second view the material is simply a liquid that has run out of time, and nothing special is happening at all. Both families reproduce important experimental facts, and neither has been able to rule the other out.

E
Experimentalists have therefore looked for shortcuts. Depositing vapour slowly onto a cooled surface, one molecular layer at a time, allows each molecule to find a comfortable position before it is buried, and produces ultrastable glasses equivalent to samples aged for thousands of years. Colloidal suspensions, in which particles a thousand times larger than molecules can be watched individually under a microscope, jam in a way that resembles the glass transition but unfolds slowly enough to record. Each approach yields data consistent with parts of both theories, which is precisely the frustration.

F
The gap between theory and practice is, meanwhile, an embarrassment to nobody in industry. The cover glass on a modern phone is strengthened by immersion in a molten salt bath, in which small sodium ions in the surface are exchanged for larger potassium ions that no longer fit, leaving the outer layer squeezed into compression so that cracks struggle to open. Optical fibre is purified until a beam can travel tens of kilometres before losing half its power. None of this required a settled theory of what a glass is; it required patient empirical chemistry.

G
Computation has recently changed the terms of the argument. Simulations can now follow every particle in a model glass for long enough to see rearrangements begin, and machine-learning methods have been trained to look at a static snapshot of positions and predict which regions will move next. That such prediction is possible at all matters, because it suggests that the frozen structure does contain information about future dynamics, even if it is not information human beings would have known how to read.

H
I find the persistence of the problem instructive rather than embarrassing. Glass is not an exotic substance produced in a national laboratory; it has been made for four thousand years, it is on the desk in front of me, and the ordinary theory of solids simply does not apply to it. There are practical stakes as well, since the same mathematics is thought to govern the packing of sand, the flow of powders, the behaviour of certain polymers and possibly the storage of information in networks of neurons. Solving glass would not merely explain a window. It would explain a whole class of systems that are stuck.

passages.title: Part 1: Reporting a lost bag at a station lost property office
passages.script:
WOMAN: Good afternoon. I think I left a bag on a train yesterday, and I was told to come to this office.
MAN: You have come to the right place. Let me open a report. Can I start with your full name?
WOMAN: It's Alison Rowntree.
MAN: Could you spell the surname for me?
WOMAN: Yes, it's R-O-W-N-T-R-E-E.
MAN: R-O-W-N-T-R-E-E. Thank you. And the best contact number?
WOMAN: My mobile is 07725 618 340.
MAN: 07725 618 340. And an address, in case we end up posting the item to you.
WOMAN: It's 46 Hartley Road, in Gosforth.
MAN: Hartley Road. And the postcode?
WOMAN: NE7 2QP.
MAN: NE7 2QP. Right. Which service were you travelling on?
WOMAN: I was coming in from Carlisle. The train was meant to leave at 6.45, but it was delayed, so we didn't arrive until nearly 8.
MAN: And that was yesterday, so Tuesday the 3rd of March.
WOMAN: Yes, Tuesday the 3rd.
MAN: Which coach were you in?
WOMAN: Coach C, near the door. I put the bag on the rack above my head instead of under the seat, and that is why I walked off without it.
MAN: That is the commonest reason we hear. Now, describe the bag for me.
WOMAN: It's a rucksack, dark green, and the zip on the front pocket is broken.
MAN: Any name label on it?
WOMAN: No label, but there is a luggage tag from a flight tied to the handle.
MAN: That's useful. And the contents?
WOMAN: A laptop. No, sorry, the laptop was in my other bag. Inside there was a camera, a pair of walking boots and a folder of photographs.
MAN: I'll record the camera as the main item, since that's the thing we would ask about if anyone else claimed the bag.
MAN: Let me see what came in from that service. Three rucksacks were handed in yesterday evening. One is black, one is grey, and one is green with a tag on the handle.
WOMAN: That sounds like mine.
MAN: I can't release it today, though. You'll need to complete the form and show identification. A driving licence or a passport is what we accept. A bank card isn't enough, because it has no photograph.
WOMAN: I have my driving licence with me.
MAN: That will do nicely. There is a charge, I should warn you. For items left on trains it's a flat fee of 12 pounds, and after 5 days an extra storage charge of 2 pounds a day is added.
WOMAN: 12 pounds is annoying, but it's cheaper than replacing a camera. Can I pay by card?
MAN: Card only, in fact. We stopped taking cash back in January.
WOMAN: And when can I collect it?
MAN: The store room opens at 9 and closes at 5.30. It's shut now, so come back tomorrow. If you arrive before 11 you'll miss the queue from the London trains.
WOMAN: I'll come at 10, then. Is there anything else I should bring?
MAN: Just the licence and your reference number, which is LP, then 4 4 7 2.
WOMAN: LP 4472. Thank you very much for your help.

passages.title: Part 2: Briefing for new volunteers at Fenwick Marshes nature reserve
passages.script:
WOMAN: Good morning, everyone. My name is Bridget, and I am the volunteer coordinator here at Fenwick Marshes. Before we go outside, I want to describe the site and how a volunteer day works.

The reserve covers 240 hectares of grazing marsh, reed bed and open water, nearly all of it farmland until the 1970s. What you see today is 50 years of work, mostly by volunteers.

Let me start with the layout, because people do get lost at first. As you come through the main gate, the visitor centre is directly in front of you and the car park is on your right. Volunteers should not use it; we need those spaces for day visitors. There is an overflow field just inside the gate on the left, and that is where you should leave your car.

Behind the visitor centre is a low wooden building with a green roof. That is the tool store, and it is where we meet every morning. Spades, saws and cutting equipment live in there.

From the tool store a gravel track runs north for about 200 metres to a fork. The left branch takes you to the boardwalk, which crosses the wet meadow and is the only safe route over that ground in winter. The right branch climbs a bank to Heron Hide, which overlooks the main lagoon and is the best spot for photography. Beyond the hide the track ends at the old pumping station, which is closed to the public but is where we keep the tractor and the trailer.

Now, the working day. We meet at the tool store at 9.15, not at 9, because that gives the wardens time to agree the tasks. We work until 1, with a break for tea at about 11. The kettle is in the visitor centre rather than the tool store, so most regulars bring a flask.

Turning to the tasks. Between October and February the main job is reed cutting, which stops the reed bed turning into woodland. In spring we switch to path repair and fencing, and in June some of you may help with the breeding bird survey, which needs separate training.

A few practical points. Bring your own boots, ideally with ankle support; the ground is uneven. Waterproof gloves are provided, and you must wear them whenever you handle cut reed. Please do not bring dogs, however well behaved, because the cattle on the marsh will chase them.

Finally, communication. Any change to the programme is posted in the volunteer group on Thursday evening, so check before you set off. If the marsh floods we cancel, which happens two or three times a winter. And there is a training day on the 12th of April, covering first aid and safe use of the brush cutter. Put that date in your diary, because we cannot let you touch a power tool until you have attended.

Right. Collect a form from the table by the door and follow me.

passages.title: Part 3: Tutorial on a survey of student study spaces
passages.script:
TUTOR: Right, let's see where you two have got to with the study space project. You collected the questionnaires last month, didn't you?
MEGAN: We did. We sent it to every first year in the department, and we got 143 completed responses back.
TUTOR: Out of how many?
OLIVER: About 510, so a response rate of just under 28 per cent.
TUTOR: That is respectable for an online survey. Megan, you looked unhappy while Oliver was saying that.
MEGAN: Well, 143 sounds like a lot until you start splitting it up. Once we divide by year group and by whether people live at home or in halls, some of our cells have fewer than 20 people in them, and I don't think we can say anything confident about groups that small.
OLIVER: I'm less bothered by the size than by the wording. Question 6 asked people how often they studied somewhere quiet, and it is obvious from the comments that half of them read it as how often they would like to.
MEGAN: That's a fair point, but a badly worded question can simply be dropped. You can't invent extra respondents.
TUTOR: You are both identifying real problems, though I would weight them differently again. My worry is neither the sample nor the wording. It is that you have treated the questionnaire as your main evidence when the richest material you have is sitting in the twelve interviews.
OLIVER: We did rather think of the interviews as a side project.
TUTOR: They shouldn't be. A survey tells you what students do. The interviews tell you why they do it, and the why is what this module actually assesses.
MEGAN: So we lead with the interview themes and use the numbers as background?
TUTOR: That would be my advice, yes.
OLIVER: I'd still like to keep the graph of where people study by time of day. That was the one result that genuinely surprised me, because the peak in the library is at 9 in the evening, not in the afternoon as I'd assumed.
MEGAN: I agree, that graph earns its place. What surprised me more was noise. I expected everyone to want silence, and in fact a third of the sample said they concentrate better with background conversation going on.
TUTOR: Which is well supported in the literature. Look at the chapter by Hartley, that's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y, in the reading list.
TUTOR: Now, the presentation itself. You have 15 minutes, plus 5 for questions, and you will be in room G12 rather than the usual seminar room, because we need the big projector.
OLIVER: Is it still the 30th of November?
TUTOR: The 30th, yes, and the written report follows two weeks after that.
MEGAN: Should we hand round copies of the questionnaire?
TUTOR: Put it in an appendix instead. Paper handouts always stop an audience listening, because everybody reads ahead. And one more thing. Say clearly at the start what you would do differently next time. Examiners reward that far more than a claim that everything went perfectly.
OLIVER: Then I'll say we would pilot the questionnaire properly. We only tested it on four people, and all four were friends of ours.
MEGAN: And I would recruit through seminars rather than by email.
TUTOR: Good. Send me the slides by the Friday before and I'll comment on them.

passages.title: Part 4: Lecture on the history of glass
passages.script:
LECTURER: Good afternoon. This is the second lecture in our series on materials that shaped ordinary life, and today the subject is glass. I want to trace it from an accident of geology to the sheet of window behind me, and I will organise the hour around four turning points.

Let me begin before human beings were involved at all, because glass occurs in nature. When certain volcanic lavas cool extremely fast, the atoms have no time to arrange themselves into a crystal, and the result is a solid with the internal disorder of a liquid. The best known example is obsidian, a black volcanic glass that fractures to leave an edge finer than surgical steel. Obsidian tools were widely traded, and because every volcano produces a slightly different chemical signature, archaeologists can trace a single blade to the mountain it came from.

Turning now to the first turning point, deliberate manufacture. The earliest man made glass we can date with confidence consists of small beads from Mesopotamia, made around 2500 BC. Producing them meant heating sand with an alkali, usually plant ash or natron, which lowers the melting point of silica far enough for a wood fired furnace to reach it. Early vessels were built up by winding a thread of molten glass around a core of clay, which was scraped out once the glass had cooled. The products were luxury objects, closer to jewellery than to tableware.

The second turning point is the blowpipe, and its importance is hard to overstate. Somewhere in the eastern Mediterranean, in the century before the Roman empire was founded, a workshop discovered that a bubble of air blown down a hollow iron tube would inflate a lump of hot glass into a vessel in seconds. Work that had occupied a craftsman for a day now took minutes. Within two generations glass had moved out of the palace and into the kitchen. Roman households stored food in glass jars, and Roman builders began setting small cast panes into window openings, although those panes were greenish and far from transparent.

I want to move on to the third turning point, which is less a technique than an institution. In 1291 the authorities in Venice ordered every glass furnace in the city to move out to the island of Murano. The reason usually given, and it is the correct one, is fire. A furnace burning day and night in a city of timber buildings was an unacceptable risk. But the move had a second consequence: concentrating the craftsmen on one island made their knowledge easier to guard, and Venice went to great lengths to stop them leaving. From Murano we get cristallo, a glass so free of the green tint of iron that it could imitate rock crystal.

The fourth turning point is chemical, and happened in England. In the 1670s a merchant named George Ravenscroft added lead oxide to the melt, and produced a heavier, softer glass with a high refractive index. Lead glass sparkled, it rang when struck, and it could be cut and engraved deeply without shattering, which is why English cut glass dominated the eighteenth century market.

Let me close with flat glass. Until the mid twentieth century a smooth window was made by casting a sheet and then grinding and polishing both surfaces, a slow process that destroyed roughly a third of the material and made large panes expensive. The solution was to float a ribbon of molten glass on a bath of molten tin, a process developed at Pilkington in the north of England and brought into full production in 1959. Tin is denser than glass and stays liquid across a wide temperature range, so the glass spreads out under its own weight and cools with two flat surfaces and no polishing at all.

Next week we turn to steel, where you will see the same pattern repeated.

passages.title: Part 4: Lecture on navigation in desert ants
passages.script:
LECTURER: Good morning. In the last two sessions we looked at navigation in migratory birds. Today I want to narrow the focus to an insect crossing a few hundred metres of gravel, and I hope to convince you that the smaller problem is the more revealing one.

Our subject is the desert ant of the North African salt pans, a genus called Cataglyphis. They live in an environment that removes almost every navigational aid we take for granted. The salt pan is flat, featureless and glaringly bright. The surface temperature can exceed 60 degrees at midday, so an ant that gets lost does not get a second chance; it dies of heat stress within minutes. Most ants find their way home by following a chemical trail, but that option is closed here, because a pheromone evaporates from hot ground almost as fast as it is deposited. And yet a forager may wander 100 metres from the nest on a twisting search for dead insects, and when it finds food it runs almost exactly straight back to a nest entrance one centimetre across.

First, then, how is that straight run possible? The mechanism is called path integration. At every moment the ant keeps an estimate of the direction and distance of home, which it updates continuously as it walks. It is not remembering the route it took; it is remembering a single vector. That is why, if you pick up an ant at the feeding site and release it 20 metres away, it will run out the same vector from the new place, arrive where the nest is not, and begin to search.

Turning now to the two quantities that vector requires: direction and distance. Direction comes from a compass, but not the magnetic kind. Sunlight scattering in the atmosphere produces a regular pattern of polarised light across the sky, and a specialised strip of receptors at the top of the ant's eye reads that pattern. The compass therefore works even when the sun is behind a dune or a cloud.

Distance is the more surprising half. It was long assumed that the ant judged distance from the flow of images across its eyes, as bees do. The evidence now points to an internal odometer that counts steps. Researchers waited until ants had walked out to a feeder, then altered their legs. One group had lengths of pig bristle glued on to make stilts, so that each step covered more ground. In another group the legs were shortened. The ants were then allowed to run home. The animals on stilts ran straight past the nest and overshot it by a predictable margin, while the ants with shortened legs stopped short and searched in the wrong place. Neither group was confused about direction; both were wrong about distance, by exactly the amount you would predict if they were counting steps.

Finally, what happens when the vector runs out and there is no nest? The ant does not wander at random. It performs a systematic search, walking in loops that form a widening spiral centred on the point where it expected the entrance to be. Close to home it also switches to a memory of the visual landmarks around the entrance, which allows it to make the final correction precisely.

Let me draw the threads together. What matters here is not the ant itself but the arithmetic of it. This animal performs continuous trigonometry with a brain of about 400,000 nerve cells, roughly one ten thousandth of the number in a mouse. That tells us something useful: sophisticated spatial behaviour does not require a large brain, only the right small set of rules. Engineers designing robots that must work where satellite positioning is unavailable, underground or on another planet, have taken the desert ant as their model for that reason.

For next week, please read the two papers on the reading list.

body.en:
## What IELTS is

IELTS (International English Language Testing System) measures English for study, work and migration. There are two versions:

- **Academic** — for university admission and professional registration. The Reading and Writing papers use academic sources and tasks.
